title: Applications of Wheatstone Bridge
short_intro: The Wheatstone bridge is a foundational electrical circuit used for precise measurement of unknown resistances by balancing potential drops across a diamond-shaped bridge network. Its practical applications extend to specialized laboratory instruments and industrial transducers.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Balanced Wheatstone bridge condition, meter bridge calculations, specific resistance determination using wire resistance.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Careful error analysis, sensitivity optimization, Carey Foster bridge for very low resistances, Callendar and Griffith's bridge for platinum resistance thermometers, and Post Office Box networks.

prerequisites: Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) and Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL)
Series and parallel combinations of resistors

concept_notes.heading: Principle of Balanced Wheatstone Bridge
bullets: A bridge consists of four arms containing resistances P, Q, R, and S arranged in a quadrilateral configuration.
A source of electromotive force is connected across one diagonal, and a sensitive galvanometer is connected across the conjugate diagonal.
The bridge is balanced when the galvanometer shows zero deflection, implying that the electric potentials at the two bridge terminals connected to the galvanometer are equal.

concept_notes.heading: Meter Bridge (Slide Wire Bridge)
bullets: It is a practical, direct-reading laboratory form of the Wheatstone bridge utilizing a uniform resistance wire of length 1 meter.
Two ratio arms are formed by dividing the wire length at the jockey contact point into lengths l and (100 - l).
It minimizes contact resistance errors by interchanging unknown and known resistances in successive measurements.

concept_notes.heading: Carey Foster Bridge
bullets: A differential variant of the Wheatstone bridge specifically designed for the precise comparison of nearly equal low resistances.
It eliminates the end-resistance errors of the bridge board by interchanging the resistances in the left and right outer gaps.
The shift in the null point is directly proportional to the difference between the two low resistances.

concept_notes.heading: Post Office Box
bullets: A compact, portable, and robust industrial form of the Wheatstone bridge packaged in a wooden box with plug-type resistance keys.
The ratio arms P and Q are typically set at fixed decimal multiples like 10, 100, or 1000 ohms.
The arm R provides adjustable resistance from 1 to 5000 ohms to achieve the most accurate bridge balance.

derivations.title: Condition for Bridge Balance
steps: Apply Kirchhoff's Current Law at junction B and D: I_1 = I_3 and I_2 = I_4.
Apply Kirchhoff's Voltage Law to closed loop ABDA: -I_1 P - I_g G + I_2 R = 0. Since I_g = 0, I_1 P = I_2 R.
Apply Kirchhoff's Voltage Law to closed loop BCDB: -I_3 Q + I_4 S + I_g G = 0. Since I_g = 0, I_3 Q = I_4 S.
Substitute I_3 = I_1 and I_4 = I_2 into the second equation: I_1 Q = I_2 S.
Divide the first equation by the fourth equation: (I_1 P)/(I_1 Q) = (I_2 R)/(I_2 S), which simplifies to P/Q = R/S.

derivations.title: Sensitivity Optimization of Wheatstone Bridge
derivations.conditions: All four bridge arms have comparable magnitudes of resistance.
steps: Define sensitivity S as the deflection of the galvanometer per unit fractional change in one of the bridge resistances.
Express the galvanometer current as a function of the bridge arms and source voltage using Thevenin's theorem.
Differentiate the galvanometer current expression with respect to the resistance of the unknown arm and equate the derivative to zero.
Show that maximum sensitivity is achieved when all four arm resistances are equal to each other, i.e., P = Q = R = S.
derivations.result: Bridge is most sensitive when P = Q = R = S

graphs_and_experiments.title: Meter Bridge Null Point Determination
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A schematic layout of a meter bridge showing a 1-meter wire AB, resistance box on left, unknown resistance on right, galvanometer, and jockey connected at balance point l.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The null point represents the exact geometric division of the wire where the ratio of resistances matches the ratio of lengths, eliminating internal resistance errors of the battery.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested via numerical questions on finding unknown resistance or shift in balance point upon parallel addition of resistors.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Galvanometer Deflection vs. Jockey Position
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A graph of galvanometer current (I_g) on the y-axis against jockey position (l) on the x-axis, showing a straight line crossing zero at the balance length l_0.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the line indicates the bridge sensitivity; a steeper slope implies higher sensitivity to small position changes near balance.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Theoretical understanding of experimental precision and choice of galvanometer.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Platinum Resistance vs. Temperature Calibration Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A linear or slightly curved plot of resistance R_t versus temperature t (^\circ\text{C}) for a platinum wire utilized in a Callendar-Griffiths bridge.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Enables direct conversion of measured resistance values into accurate thermodynamic temperature readings.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Problems involving temperature coefficients of resistance and thermal bridge calibration.

solved_numericals.question: In a meter bridge, the null point is found at a distance of 40 cm from the left end when a resistance of 12 ohm is connected in the right gap. Find the unknown resistance in the left gap.
solution_steps: Identify the known parameters: right gap resistance S = 12 ohm, balancing length l = 40 cm.
Determine the remaining length of the wire: 100 - l = 100 - 40 = 60 cm.
Use the meter bridge formula: P / Q = l / (100 - l), where P is the unknown resistance in the left gap and Q corresponds to the right gap resistance S.

solved_numericals.question: Four resistors of resistance 2 ohm, 2 ohm, 2 ohm, and 3 ohm are connected to form the first three and fourth arms of a Wheatstone bridge. What resistance must be connected in parallel with the 3 ohm resistor to balance the bridge?
solution_steps: Let the arms be P = 2 ohm, Q = 2 ohm, R = 2 ohm, and the fourth arm has S' = 3 ohm initially.
For a balanced bridge, the condition is P / Q = R / S_eq.
Substitute the values: 2 / 2 = 2 / S_eq, which gives S_eq = 2 ohm.
Let the required parallel resistance be x. The equivalent resistance of 3 ohm and x in parallel is given by (3 * x) / (3 + x) = 2.
Solve for x: 3x = 2(3 + x) => 3x = 6 + 2x => x = 6 ohm.

solved_numericals.question: In a Carey Foster bridge, two nearly equal resistances P and Q are placed in the inner gaps. With a standard resistance of 1.0 ohm in the left outer gap and an unknown resistance in the right outer gap, the null point is obtained at 45 cm. When the resistances in the outer gaps are interchanged, the null point shifts by 2 cm. If the resistance of the bridge wire is 0.1 ohm per cm, calculate the value of the unknown resistance.
solution_steps: Recall the Carey Foster bridge relation for resistance difference: S - R = \delta l \times \rho, where \delta l is the shift in null point and \rho is resistance per unit length.
Identify the given values: \delta l = 2 cm, \rho = 0.1 \Omega/\text{cm}, and the known resistance R = 1.0 \0hm.
Substitute R = 1.0 \Omega into the equation: S - 1.0 = 0.2.
Solve for the unknown resistance S: S = 1.0 + 0.2 = 1.2 \Omega.

assumptions_and_limitations: Connecting wire and terminal resistances (end errors) are neglected unless specialized calibration bridges like Carey Foster are used.
Heating effects due to current flow through the bridge arms are assumed negligible so that resistances remain constant during measurement.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Interchanging the battery and galvanometer terminals alters the balanced condition of a Wheatstone bridge.
common_misconceptions.correct: Interchanging the battery and galvanometer leaves the balance condition P/Q = R/S entirely unchanged.
common_misconceptions.why: The bridge balance symmetry relies strictly on the ratio of adjacent and opposite arm resistances, which remains invariant under interchange of conjugate diagonals.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A Wheatstone bridge can accurately measure extremely low resistances without special modifications.
common_misconceptions.correct: Standard Wheatstone bridges cannot measure very low resistances accurately due to the comparable magnitude of lead and contact resistances.
common_misconceptions.why: Contact resistances become a significant fraction of very low unknown resistances, necessitating Kelvin's double bridge instead.

quick_revision: Balanced Wheatstone bridge condition: P / Q = R / S with zero galvanometer current.
Meter Bridge Unknown Resistance: S = R \left(\frac{100 - l}{l}\right)
